claims.text: A moderate level of surface oxidation and hydroxyl coverage optimizes ethanol adsorption and activation on Pt-based nanoscale catalysts.
Moderate surface oxidation promotes complete 12-electron ethanol oxidation.
Surface oxide or hydroxyl coverage promotes C–C bond cleavage during ethanol oxidation.
Surface oxide or hydroxyl coverage mitigates poisoning by reaction intermediates.
Systematic potential cycling from approximately 0.05 to 1.2 V versus RHE can generate a controlled level of surface oxide and hydroxyl species.
The extent of surface Pt oxide and hydroxyl species modulates the local electronic structure of active sites.
Induced surface oxides and hydroxyls modify the binding energies of ethanol and its intermediates.
The binding-energy changes caused by surface oxides and hydroxyls lower the barrier for C–C bond cleavage.
Induced surface oxides and hydroxyls lower the barrier for the overall 12-electron oxidation pathway.
Induced surface oxides and hydroxyls prevent the accumulation of carbonaceous poisoning species.
An optimal coverage balances oxidative activation of ethanol against preservation of active-site integrity.
Moderate oxide or hydroxyl coverage will produce higher current density than a minimally pre-treated, predominantly metallic baseline.
Moderate oxide or hydroxyl coverage will increase selectivity toward complete oxidation products such as CO2.
Moderate oxide or hydroxyl coverage will improve catalyst durability relative to the minimally pre-treated baseline.
Excessive oxide or hydroxyl formation lowers activity through over-oxidation and possible catalyst degradation.
The proposed effect applies to ambient-temperature ethanol oxidation in acidic electrolytes.
Extreme potential cycling can cause irreversible structural changes or degradation that invalidate the proposed mechanism.
